subject: Business Law & Practice
title: Removing a company director: ordinary resolution and special notice
scenario: Maya holds 60% of the shares in Fernhill Joinery Ltd, a private company limited by shares that has adopted the model articles without amendment. She wants to remove Tom, one of the company's three directors. Tom has a written service contract with the company that still has two years to run. Maya would prefer to avoid a meeting and asks whether she can simply circulate a written resolution to the shareholders.
stem: Which of the following best describes how Tom can be removed as a director?

options.A: By a written resolution signed by members holding at least 75% of the voting rights.
options.B: By a special resolution passed at a general meeting called on at least 14 clear days' notice.
options.C: By an ordinary resolution passed at a general meeting, special notice of the resolution having been given to the company at least 28 days before the meeting.
options.D: By a resolution of the board passed by the other two directors.
options.E: He cannot be removed until his service contract expires, because the company would otherwise be in breach of contract.

explanation:
Under s.168(1) Companies Act 2006 a company may remove a director by ordinary resolution at a meeting, notwithstanding anything in any agreement with the director. Special notice is required (s.168(2)), which means notice of the intention to move the resolution must be given to the company at least 28 days before the meeting (s.312(1)). A written resolution cannot be used for a s.168 removal (s.288(2)(a)), so a meeting is unavoidable.

A is wrong: s.288(2)(a) prohibits removing a director under s.168 by written resolution, and in any case only an ordinary (simple majority) resolution is needed.
B is wrong: an ordinary resolution suffices; a special resolution is not required.
D is wrong: the statutory power of removal belongs to the members; the model articles give the board no power to remove a fellow director.
E is wrong: s.168(1) applies notwithstanding any agreement; Tom's contract only preserves any claim to compensation or damages (s.168(5)).
key_rule: A director can be removed by ordinary resolution at a general meeting on special notice (28 days to the company), and never by written resolution.
authority: Companies Act 2006, ss.168, 288(2)(a) and 312

why_wrong.A: s.288(2)(a) prohibits removing a director under s.168 by written resolution, and in any case only an ordinary (simple majority) resolution is needed.
why_wrong.B: an ordinary resolution suffices; a special resolution is not required.
why_wrong.D: the statutory power of removal belongs to the members; the model articles give the board no power to remove a fellow director.
why_wrong.E: s.168(1) applies notwithstanding any agreement; Tom's contract only preserves any claim to compensation or damages (s.168(5)).

subject: Dispute Resolution
title: Time limit for serving a claim form within the jurisdiction (CPR 7.5)
scenario: A solicitor acts for a claimant in a contract claim against a supplier based in Leeds. The court issued the claim form on 10 February 2026. The solicitor intends to serve the claim form on the defendant at its registered office by first class post.
stem: Which of the following correctly states the latest point by which the claimant must act to serve the claim form in time?

options.A: The claim form must be received by the defendant before midnight on 10 June 2026.
options.B: The claim form must be posted before 12.00 midnight on 10 June 2026.
options.C: The claim form must be served within six months of the date of issue, i.e. by 10 August 2026.
options.D: The claim form must be served within 14 days of the date of issue.
options.E: The claim form must be deemed served by 10 June 2026, so posting it on 10 June 2026 would be too late.

explanation:
CPR 7.5(1) requires a claimant serving within the jurisdiction to complete the 'step required' for the chosen method of service before 12.00 midnight on the calendar day four months after the date of issue. For first class post the step is posting. Four months after 10 February 2026 is 10 June 2026, so the claim form must be posted before midnight on that day.

A is wrong: the rule turns on the claimant's step (posting), not on receipt by the defendant.
C is wrong: six months applies only where the claim form is served out of the jurisdiction (CPR 7.5(2)).
D is wrong: 14 days is the period for serving particulars of claim after the claim form, where they are served separately (CPR 7.4(1)(b)).
E is wrong: deemed service of the claim form is not the test under CPR 7.5; completing the step in time is what matters.
key_rule: A claim form served in England and Wales must have the relevant step (e.g. posting) completed before midnight on the calendar day four months after issue.

why_wrong.A: The rule turns on the claimant's step (posting), not on receipt by the defendant.
why_wrong.C: Six months applies only where the claim form is served out of the jurisdiction (CPR 7.5(2)).
why_wrong.D: 14 days is the period for serving particulars of claim after the claim form, where they are served separately (CPR 7.4(1)(b)).
why_wrong.E: Deemed service of the claim form is not the test under CPR 7.5; completing the step in time is what matters.

subject: Contract
title: Counter-offers and the rejection of an original offer
scenario: On Monday Rhys emails Ola offering to sell her his vintage campervan for £18,000, adding: 'This offer is open until Friday.' On Wednesday Ola replies: 'I will pay £16,500 for it.' Rhys replies the same day: 'No, sorry.' On Thursday Ola emails: 'Fine, I accept your offer at £18,000.' Rhys has meanwhile decided to keep the campervan and refuses to sell.
stem: Which of the following best describes the legal position?

options.A: There is a contract at £18,000, because Rhys said his offer would remain open until Friday.
options.B: There is a contract at £16,500, because that was the last price proposed before acceptance.
options.C: There is a contract at £18,000, because Ola's Wednesday email was only a request for information.
options.D: There is no contract: Ola's counter-offer rejected Rhys's offer, so her Thursday email is a fresh offer that Rhys is free to refuse.
options.E: There is no contract, because an acceptance sent by email is not effective until the offeror reads it.

explanation:
A counter-offer operates as a rejection of the original offer, which cannot afterwards be revived by a purported acceptance (Hyde v Wrench (1840)). Ola's Wednesday email proposed a new price and so was a counter-offer. Rhys's original offer was destroyed, and Ola's Thursday email can only be a new offer, which Rhys may decline.

A is wrong: a promise to keep an offer open is not binding without consideration, and in any event the counter-offer ended the offer.
B is wrong: Rhys expressly rejected the £16,500 counter-offer, so there was nothing to accept at that price.
C is wrong: 'I will pay £16,500' is a firm proposal of new terms, not a mere enquiry about whether Rhys would accept less.
E is wrong: the timing of email acceptance is irrelevant here, because there was no subsisting offer to accept.
key_rule: A counter-offer rejects and destroys the original offer, which cannot then be accepted.
authority: Hyde v Wrench (1840) 49 ER 132; [1840] EWHC Ch J90

why_wrong.A: A promise to keep an offer open is not binding without consideration, and in any event the counter-offer ended the offer.
why_wrong.B: Rhys expressly rejected the £16,500 counter-offer, so there was nothing to accept at that price.
why_wrong.C: 'I will pay £16,500' is a firm proposal of new terms, not a mere enquiry about whether Rhys would accept less.
why_wrong.E: The timing of email acceptance is irrelevant here, because there was no subsisting offer to accept.

subject: Tort
title: Occupiers' liability to skilled visitors and risks incident to their calling
scenario: Dana owns and runs a café. A wall socket behind the counter has started sparking, so she calls out Kofi, a qualified electrician, and tells him exactly what the fault is. Kofi decides to work on the socket without isolating the electricity supply, to save time. He receives an electric shock and is injured. There is nothing else wrong with the premises.
stem: Which of the following best describes Dana's likely liability to Kofi under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957?

options.A: Dana is unlikely to be liable, because an occupier may expect a person exercising his calling to appreciate and guard against special risks ordinarily incident to it.
options.B: Dana is likely to be liable, because the common duty of care owed to visitors cannot vary according to the skill of the visitor.
options.C: Dana is likely to be liable under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984, because Kofi exceeded the scope of his invitation and became a trespasser.
options.D: Dana is not liable solely because she warned Kofi about the fault, and a warning always discharges the occupier's duty.
options.E: Dana is liable, because an occupier is strictly liable for injuries caused by the state of the premises.

explanation:
The common duty of care takes account of the care to be expected of the visitor. Under s.2(3)(b) OLA 1957 an occupier may expect a person, in the exercise of his calling, to appreciate and guard against any special risks ordinarily incident to it, so far as the occupier leaves him free to do so. The risk of a shock from a live socket is exactly the kind of risk an electrician is expected to guard against.

B is wrong: s.2(3) expressly makes the visitor's expected degree of care relevant, so the duty does vary with the visitor.
C is wrong: Kofi was on the premises to do the very job he was invited to do; he was a visitor, so the 1957 Act applies.
D is wrong: under s.2(4)(a) a warning does not by itself absolve the occupier unless it was enough to enable the visitor to be reasonably safe; Dana escapes liability because of s.2(3)(b), not because a warning is automatically enough.
E is wrong: liability under the 1957 Act is fault-based (a duty of reasonable care), not strict.
key_rule: An occupier may expect a skilled visitor to guard against the special risks ordinarily incident to their calling (OLA 1957 s.2(3)(b)).
authority: Occupiers' Liability Act 1957, s.2(3)(b) and s.2(4)(a); Roles v Nathan [1963] 1 WLR 1117

why_wrong.B: S.2(3) expressly makes the visitor's expected degree of care relevant, so the duty does vary with the visitor.
why_wrong.C: Kofi was on the premises to do the very job he was invited to do; he was a visitor, so the 1957 Act applies.
why_wrong.D: Under s.2(4)(a) a warning does not by itself absolve the occupier unless it was enough to enable the visitor to be reasonably safe; Dana escapes liability because of s.2(3)(b), not because a warning is automatically enough.
why_wrong.E: Liability under the 1957 Act is fault-based (a duty of reasonable care), not strict.

subject: Constitutional & Administrative Law
title: Judicial review time limits: promptly and within three months
scenario: On 2 March 2026 a local council revoked Bilal's street-trading licence. The decision has nothing to do with planning. Bilal instructs a solicitor in late May 2026. He has a letter from the council's legal department saying that the council 'will not take any point on delay' provided any judicial review claim is filed by 31 July 2026.
stem: Which of the following best describes the time limit for Bilal's claim for judicial review?

options.A: The claim may be filed at any time within six months of the decision.
options.B: The claim may be filed by 31 July 2026, because the council has agreed to extend time.
options.C: The claim must be filed within six weeks of the decision, so it is already out of time.
options.D: Provided the claim is filed within three months of the decision, the court cannot refuse it on the ground of delay.
options.E: The claim must be filed promptly and in any event not later than three months after the grounds first arose, and the council's letter cannot extend that time.

explanation:
CPR 54.5(1) requires a judicial review claim form to be filed promptly and in any event not later than three months after the grounds to make the claim first arose. CPR 54.5(2) provides that these time limits may not be extended by agreement between the parties. Bilal should therefore file without delay and in any event by early June 2026; only the court can extend time.

A is wrong: there is no general six-month period for judicial review.
B is wrong: CPR 54.5(2) expressly prevents the parties extending time by agreement.
C is wrong: the six-week limit in CPR 54.5(5) applies to decisions under the planning Acts, which this is not.
D is wrong: the duty to act promptly is separate from the three-month long-stop, so a claim filed within three months can still be refused for lack of promptness.
key_rule: A judicial review claim must be filed promptly and within three months of the grounds arising, and the parties cannot extend this by agreement.

why_wrong.A: There is no general six-month period for judicial review.
why_wrong.B: CPR 54.5(2) expressly prevents the parties extending time by agreement.
why_wrong.C: The six-week limit in CPR 54.5(5) applies to decisions under the planning Acts, which this is not.
why_wrong.D: The duty to act promptly is separate from the three-month long-stop, so a claim filed within three months can still be refused for lack of promptness.

subject: Ethics & Professional Conduct
title: Acting for clients competing for the same objective (SRA Code 6.2)
scenario: Two long-standing clients of a commercial property firm, Harbour Coffee Ltd and Kiln Bakery Ltd, separately ask the firm to act for them in bidding for the lease of the same high-street unit. The landlord's agent is running a sealed-bid process and only one lease will be granted. Both clients want to keep using the firm.
stem: Which of the following best describes whether the firm may act for both clients?

options.A: The firm must decline to act for both, because a solicitor may never act where there is a conflict of interest between clients.
options.B: The firm may act for both if both clients give informed consent, given or evidenced in writing, effective safeguards protect their confidential information where appropriate, and the firm is satisfied it is reasonable to act for both.
options.C: The firm may act for both if both clients consent orally, as written consent is needed only where there is litigation.
options.D: The firm may act for both without consent, because there is no conflict unless the clients are in dispute with each other.
options.E: The firm may act only for whichever client instructed it first, and must turn the other away.

explanation:
Paragraph 6.2 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors prohibits acting where there is a conflict, or significant risk of conflict, unless an exception applies. One exception is where the clients are 'competing for the same objective', as two bidders for the same lease are. Even then, all clients must give informed consent, given or evidenced in writing; effective safeguards must be put in place to protect confidential information where appropriate; and the solicitor must be satisfied it is reasonable to act for all of them.

A is wrong: paragraph 6.2 allows two exceptions (substantially common interest and competing for the same objective), so a conflict is not an absolute bar.
C is wrong: the consent must be given or evidenced in writing, whatever the type of matter.
D is wrong: a conflict exists because the clients' interests in the same lease are adverse; a dispute between them is not needed.
E is wrong: the Code contains no 'first come, first served' rule.
key_rule: A solicitor may act for clients competing for the same objective only with all clients' informed written consent, appropriate confidentiality safeguards, and where it is reasonable to act.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, para 6.2(b)

why_wrong.A: Paragraph 6.2 allows two exceptions (substantially common interest and competing for the same objective), so a conflict is not an absolute bar.
why_wrong.C: The consent must be given or evidenced in writing, whatever the type of matter.
why_wrong.D: A conflict exists because the clients' interests in the same lease are adverse; a dispute between them is not needed.
why_wrong.E: The Code contains no 'first come, first served' rule.

subject: Property Practice
title: Priority period of an official search of registered land (OS1)
scenario: A solicitor acts for a buyer of a registered freehold house, with a mortgage. Before completion she applies for an official search of the whole of the title with priority (form OS1), and the result reveals no adverse entries. Completion takes place a week later.
stem: Which of the following best describes the protection the official search gives the buyer?

options.A: It protects the buyer's priority for 30 calendar days from the date of completion.
options.B: It freezes the register, so the Land Registry cannot make any entry on the title during the priority period.
options.C: If the buyer's application to register the transfer is received by the Land Registry within the priority period, which ends at midnight at the end of the 30th working day after the search application is entered on the day list, it takes priority over any entry made in the meantime.
options.D: It protects the buyer for 30 working days from the date of exchange of contracts.
options.E: It is relevant only to unregistered land, so it gives a buyer of registered land no priority.

explanation:
Under rule 131 of the Land Registration Rules 2003, the priority period begins when the application for an official search is entered on the day list and ends at midnight marking the end of the thirtieth working day afterwards. If the buyer (and lender) lodge their application for registration within that period, it takes priority over any entry made on the register during the period. The buyer's solicitor must therefore diarise the end of the priority period and apply to register before it expires.

A is wrong: the period runs in working days from when the search application is entered on the day list, not calendar days from completion.
B is wrong: entries can still be made on the register; they are simply postponed to the searcher's application if that is lodged in time.
D is wrong: the period does not run from exchange.
E is wrong: the OS1 search is a registered-land search; unregistered land uses a Land Charges Department search with its own protection period.
key_rule: An official search with priority protects a buyer who applies to register within 30 working days of the search application being entered on the day list.
authority: Land Registration Rules 2003 (SI 2003/1417), r.131 (definition of 'priority period'); Land Registration Act 2002, s.72

why_wrong.A: The period runs in working days from when the search application is entered on the day list, not calendar days from completion.
why_wrong.B: Entries can still be made on the register; they are simply postponed to the searcher's application if that is lodged in time.
why_wrong.D: The period does not run from exchange.
why_wrong.E: The OS1 search is a registered-land search; unregistered land uses a Land Charges Department search with its own protection period.

subject: Wills & Administration of Estates
title: Gifts to a witness's spouse under section 15 Wills Act 1837
scenario: Rosalind signed her will in the presence of two witnesses: her neighbour, Priti, and Gareth, the husband of her close friend Lena. Gareth and Lena were married at the time. The will leaves £20,000 to Lena and the residue to Rosalind's nephew. No one else witnessed the will. Rosalind has now died, and the will was otherwise validly executed.
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of Gareth having witnessed the will?

options.A: The will is valid, but the gift of £20,000 to Lena is void.
options.B: The whole will is invalid, because a witness's spouse is a beneficiary.
options.C: The gift to Lena is valid, because Gareth himself takes nothing under the will.
options.D: The gift to Lena is valid if she did not know that Gareth had witnessed the will.
options.E: The gift of £20,000 passes to Gareth instead of Lena.

explanation:
Section 15 Wills Act 1837 provides that where a person attests a will under which a beneficial gift is made to that person or to their spouse (or civil partner), the gift is void as regards that person or spouse. The witness remains a competent witness, so the will itself is valid. The £20,000 falls into residue and passes to the nephew. (Had there been a third, independent witness, s.1 Wills Act 1968 would have let the gift stand.)

B is wrong: s.15 voids the gift only, not the will; Gareth is still a valid witness.
C is wrong: s.15 expressly extends to the witness's spouse.
D is wrong: the beneficiary's knowledge is irrelevant; the rule operates automatically.
E is wrong: nothing in s.15 redirects the gift to the witness; the failed gift falls into residue.
key_rule: A gift to an attesting witness or their spouse or civil partner is void, but the will remains valid.
authority: Wills Act 1837, s.15; Wills Act 1968, s.1

why_wrong.B: S.15 voids the gift only, not the will; Gareth is still a valid witness.
why_wrong.C: S.15 expressly extends to the witness's spouse.
why_wrong.D: The beneficiary's knowledge is irrelevant; the rule operates automatically.
why_wrong.E: Nothing in s.15 redirects the gift to the witness; the failed gift falls into residue.

subject: Wills & Administration of Estates
title: Intestacy and the 28-day spousal survivorship rule
scenario: Arjun died intestate on 1 May 2026, domiciled in England. He was survived by his wife, Neha, and their two adult children. Neha was seriously ill and died 19 days after Arjun. Arjun's estate consists of personal chattels and investments well in excess of the statutory legacy.
stem: Which of the following best describes how Arjun's estate will be distributed?

options.A: Neha's estate takes the personal chattels, the statutory legacy with interest, and half of the remaining residue; the children take the other half on the statutory trusts.
options.B: Neha's estate takes the whole of Arjun's estate absolutely, because she survived him.
options.C: Arjun's estate is divided equally between Neha's estate and the two children.
options.D: Neha is treated as not having survived Arjun, so the whole estate is held on the statutory trusts for the two children.
options.E: The estate passes to the Crown as bona vacantia, because the spouse died before the estate was administered.

explanation:
Section 46(2A) Administration of Estates Act 1925 provides that where the intestate's spouse or civil partner survives the intestate but dies within 28 days beginning with the day of death, the spouse is treated as not having survived. Neha died 19 days after Arjun, so she is ignored. Arjun leaves issue but no surviving spouse for intestacy purposes, so under s.46(1)(ii) the whole residuary estate is held on the statutory trusts for his children.

A is wrong: this describes the entitlement of a spouse who qualifies (s.46(1)(i)); Neha does not, because of the 28-day rule.
B is wrong: even a qualifying spouse does not take everything where the intestate leaves issue, and Neha is in any case treated as predeceasing.
C is wrong: intestacy contains no rule of equal division between spouse and children.
E is wrong: bona vacantia arises only where no one entitled survives; the children take.
key_rule: On intestacy a spouse or civil partner who dies within 28 days of the intestate is treated as not having survived.
authority: Administration of Estates Act 1925, s.46(1) and (2A)

why_wrong.A: This describes the entitlement of a spouse who qualifies (s.46(1)(i)); Neha does not, because of the 28-day rule.
why_wrong.B: Even a qualifying spouse does not take everything where the intestate leaves issue, and Neha is in any case treated as predeceasing.
why_wrong.C: Intestacy contains no rule of equal division between spouse and children.
why_wrong.E: Bona vacantia arises only where no one entitled survives; the children take.

subject: Solicitors Accounts
title: Transferring client money for costs: bill first (SRA Accounts Rules 4.3)
scenario: A firm acting for a client on the purchase of a house holds £3,000 in client account, received from the client 'on account of costs' at the start of the matter. The fee earner has now done work worth £1,200 plus VAT (£1,440 in total). She wants the cashier to transfer £1,440 to the business (office) account today and plans to send the client a bill next week.
stem: Which of the following best describes what the firm must do before transferring the money?

options.A: Nothing: money received on account of costs is business money as soon as it is received.
options.B: Telephone the client to tell them about the transfer; written notification is not required.
options.C: Transfer the whole £3,000 to the business account to save multiple transfers, and refund any surplus at the end of the matter.
options.D: Leave the money in client account until the matter ends, because client money can never be used to pay the firm's costs.
options.E: Give the client a bill or other written notification of the costs first, and then transfer only the specific sum identified in it.

explanation:
Money held for fees before a bill is delivered is client money (rule 2.1(d) SRA Accounts Rules) and must be kept in client account. Under rule 4.3, where client money is to be used to pay the firm's costs, the firm must give a bill of costs or other written notification of the costs incurred to the client before transferring any client money, and the transfer must be for the specific sum identified and covered by funds held for that client.

A is wrong: unbilled money on account of costs is client money under rule 2.1(d).
B is wrong: rule 4.3 requires a bill or other written notification; a phone call is not enough.
C is wrong: only the specific sum billed may be transferred; moving unbilled client money to business account breaches rules 4.1 and 4.3.
D is wrong: client money can be used to pay costs once rule 4.3 has been complied with.
key_rule: Client money may be transferred to pay the firm's costs only after a bill or other written notification has been given, and only for the specific sum identified.
authority: SRA Accounts Rules, rules 2.1(d), 4.1 and 4.3

why_wrong.A: Unbilled money on account of costs is client money under rule 2.1(d).
why_wrong.B: Rule 4.3 requires a bill or other written notification; a phone call is not enough.
why_wrong.C: Only the specific sum billed may be transferred; moving unbilled client money to business account breaches rules 4.1 and 4.3.
why_wrong.D: Client money can be used to pay costs once rule 4.3 has been complied with.

subject: Land Law
title: Freehold covenants: the burden of a positive covenant does not run
scenario: In 2012 Ivy sold part of her registered freehold land to Ben. In the transfer Ivy covenanted, for herself and her successors in title, to maintain the boundary fence between the two plots. In 2020 Ivy sold her retained land to Carl. Carl claims no right or benefit under the 2012 transfer. The fence has now collapsed, and Carl refuses to repair it. Ben wants to sue Carl.
stem: Which of the following best describes whether Ben can enforce the covenant against Carl?

options.A: Yes, because equity will enforce a covenant against a successor with notice under the rule in Tulk v Moxhay.
options.B: No, because the burden of a positive covenant does not run with freehold land to bind a successor in title.
options.C: Yes, because section 79 Law of Property Act 1925 makes covenants relating to land bind successors in title.
options.D: Yes, because section 78 Law of Property Act 1925 passes the covenant to successors.
options.E: Yes, provided the covenant was entered on the register of Carl's title.

explanation:
A covenant to maintain a fence is positive: it requires expenditure. In Rhone v Stephens [1994] 2 AC 310 the House of Lords confirmed that the burden of a positive covenant does not run with freehold land, either at law or in equity. Carl was not a party to the covenant and takes no reciprocal benefit (so the Halsall v Brizell benefit-and-burden principle does not help), so Ben cannot enforce it against him. Ben's remedy, if any, lies against Ivy on her personal covenant.

A is wrong: Tulk v Moxhay applies only to restrictive (negative) covenants.
C is wrong: Rhone v Stephens held that s.79 LPA 1925 is a word-saving provision and does not make the burden of positive covenants run.
D is wrong: s.78 concerns the running of the benefit, not the burden.
E is wrong: entry on the register cannot make the burden of a positive covenant bind a successor.
key_rule: The burden of a positive freehold covenant does not run to bind successors in title, at law or in equity.
authority: Rhone v Stephens [1994] UKHL 3; [1994] 2 AC 310

why_wrong.A: Tulk v Moxhay applies only to restrictive (negative) covenants.
why_wrong.C: Rhone v Stephens held that s.79 LPA 1925 is a word-saving provision and does not make the burden of positive covenants run.
why_wrong.D: S.78 concerns the running of the benefit, not the burden.
why_wrong.E: Entry on the register cannot make the burden of a positive covenant bind a successor.

subject: Trusts
title: The rule in Saunders v Vautier: ending a trust early
scenario: By her will, Sofia's grandmother left £60,000 to trustees 'on trust for my granddaughter Sofia absolutely, but the trustees shall not pay the capital to her until she reaches the age of 25; until then the income is to be accumulated and added to the capital.' Sofia is now 19, has full mental capacity, and asks the trustees to transfer the whole fund to her. No one else has any interest under the trust.
stem: Which of the following best describes Sofia's position?

options.A: She must wait until she is 25, because the trustees are bound to give effect to the testator's clearly expressed wishes.
options.B: She can obtain the fund now only if the court approves a variation under the Variation of Trusts Act 1958.
options.C: She can require the trustees to transfer the capital and accumulated income to her now, because she is an adult of full capacity with a vested and absolute interest in the whole fund.
options.D: She must wait until she is 21.
options.E: She can require payment of the accumulated income now, but not the capital.

explanation:
Under the rule in Saunders v Vautier (1841), a beneficiary (or beneficiaries acting together) who is of full age and capacity and absolutely entitled to the trust property can call for it and bring the trust to an end, even though the trust instrument postpones enjoyment. The gift here is to Sofia 'absolutely'; the reference to age 25 merely postpones payment and does not make her interest contingent. As she is over 18 and the only person interested, she can call for the whole fund. Contrast a gift 'to Sofia if she attains 25', which would be contingent and could not be called for at 19.

A is wrong: a direction merely postponing enjoyment does not bind a sui juris beneficiary who is absolutely entitled.
B is wrong: court approval under the 1958 Act is needed only where some beneficiaries cannot consent (for example minors or unborn persons); none exist here.
D is wrong: the age of majority is 18; 21 was the age of majority when Saunders v Vautier was decided.
E is wrong: Sofia is entitled to both income and capital, so she can call for the whole fund.
key_rule: Adult beneficiaries of full capacity who are together absolutely entitled can call for the trust property and end the trust.
authority: Saunders v Vautier (1841) 4 Beav 115; 49 ER 282

why_wrong.A: A direction merely postponing enjoyment does not bind a sui juris beneficiary who is absolutely entitled.
why_wrong.B: Court approval under the 1958 Act is needed only where some beneficiaries cannot consent (for example minors or unborn persons); none exist here.
why_wrong.D: The age of majority is 18; 21 was the age of majority when Saunders v Vautier was decided.
why_wrong.E: Sofia is entitled to both income and capital, so she can call for the whole fund.

subject: Criminal Law
title: The test for dishonesty after Ivey v Genting and R v Barton
scenario: Leon, a self-employed builder, finishes a kitchen refit for a client and sends an invoice that includes £900 for materials he knows he never bought or used. He is charged with fraud by false representation. In interview he says that 'everyone in the trade pads their invoices' and that he did not think anyone would regard it as dishonest.
stem: Which of the following best describes how the court will decide whether Leon acted dishonestly?

options.A: The jury will first establish Leon's actual knowledge or belief as to the facts, and then decide whether his conduct was dishonest by the standards of ordinary decent people; Leon's own view of those standards is no defence.
options.B: Leon is dishonest only if he realised that ordinary decent people would regard what he did as dishonest.
options.C: Leon is not dishonest if he genuinely believed that padding invoices was acceptable practice in the building trade.
options.D: Dishonesty is irrelevant, because fraud by false representation requires only a false representation and an intention to make a gain.
options.E: Leon can be dishonest only if the client actually suffered a financial loss.

explanation:
Fraud by false representation requires that the defendant 'dishonestly' makes a false representation intending to make a gain or cause loss (s.2(1) Fraud Act 2006). The test for dishonesty in criminal cases is the one set out in Ivey v Genting Casinos [2017] UKSC 67 and confirmed in R v Barton and Booth [2020] EWCA Crim 575. The fact-finder first establishes the defendant's actual state of knowledge or belief as to the facts, then decides whether the conduct was dishonest by the objective standards of ordinary decent people. There is no further requirement that the defendant appreciated that his conduct was dishonest by those standards. Leon knew he had not used the materials, so his belief about trade practice does not help him.

B is wrong: this is the second, subjective limb of R v Ghosh, which no longer applies.
C is wrong: a defendant's belief about the honesty of his conduct, as opposed to his belief about the facts, is not the test.
D is wrong: dishonesty is an express element of s.2(1)(a) Fraud Act 2006.
E is wrong: s.2 requires only an intention to make a gain or cause loss (or expose another to a risk of loss); actual loss is not needed.
key_rule: Dishonesty is judged by the standards of ordinary decent people, applied to the defendant's actual knowledge or belief as to the facts (Ivey; Barton).
authority: Ivey v Genting Casinos (UK) Ltd [2017] UKSC 67; R v Barton and Booth [2020] EWCA Crim 575; Fraud Act 2006, s.2

why_wrong.C: A defendant's belief about the honesty of his conduct, as opposed to his belief about the facts, is not the test.
why_wrong.D: Dishonesty is an express element of s.2(1)(a) Fraud Act 2006.
why_wrong.E: S.2 requires only an intention to make a gain or cause loss (or expose another to a risk of loss); actual loss is not needed.

subject: Criminal Practice
title: Delaying access to legal advice at the police station (PACE s.58)
scenario: Kemi is arrested on suspicion of burglary of a warehouse and taken to a police station, where she asks to speak to a solicitor. The police believe two accomplices have not yet been arrested. An inspector authorises a delay in Kemi's access to a solicitor, on the ground that a solicitor's call might alert the accomplices.
stem: Which of the following best describes whether the delay is lawful?

options.A: It is lawful, because an inspector may authorise delay for any indictable offence.
options.B: It is lawful, because a detained person has no right to legal advice until she has been charged.
options.C: It is unlawful, because access to legal advice can never be delayed once requested.
options.D: It is unlawful, because delay may be authorised only by an officer of at least the rank of superintendent, and then only for an indictable offence on the grounds set out in s.58(8) PACE.
options.E: It is lawful, and access may be delayed for up to 96 hours.

explanation:
Section 58 PACE 1984 gives a person arrested and held in custody the right, on request, to consult a solicitor privately at any time. Delay is permitted only where the person is in police detention for an indictable offence and an officer of at least the rank of superintendent authorises it (s.58(6)), on reasonable grounds such as a belief that exercising the right will lead to the alerting of other suspects not yet arrested (s.58(8)(b)). Access must in any case be allowed within 36 hours of the relevant time (s.58(5)). Burglary is indictable and the ground relied on is a permitted one, but an inspector is below the required rank, so the authorisation is invalid.

A is wrong: an inspector is below the rank of superintendent.
B is wrong: the s.58 right applies from when a person is arrested and held in custody, not just after charge.
C is wrong: s.58(6) and (8) allow delay in limited circumstances.
E is wrong: the maximum delay under s.58(5) is 36 hours from the relevant time; 96 hours is the outer limit of detention without charge, which is a different rule.
key_rule: Access to a solicitor may be delayed only for an indictable offence, on superintendent authority, on the s.58(8) grounds, and for no more than 36 hours.
authority: Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984, s.58

why_wrong.A: An inspector is below the rank of superintendent.
why_wrong.B: The s.58 right applies from when a person is arrested and held in custody, not just after charge.
why_wrong.C: S.58(6) and (8) allow delay in limited circumstances.
why_wrong.E: The maximum delay under s.58(5) is 36 hours from the relevant time; 96 hours is the outer limit of detention without charge, which is a different rule.

subject: Business Law & Practice
title: Declaring an interest in a proposed transaction (CA 2006 s.177)
scenario: Priya Nair is one of four directors of Halden Interiors Ltd. The board plans to approve a five-year lease of a warehouse from Moorgate Holdings Ltd at its meeting next week. Priya's husband owns 60% of the shares in Moorgate Holdings Ltd. None of the other directors knows of this, and Priya has said nothing because she personally holds no shares in Moorgate and will not be signing the lease.
stem: Which of the following best describes Priya's duty under the Companies Act 2006?

options.A: She has no duty to declare anything, because the shareholding belongs to her husband and not to her.
options.B: She must declare the nature and extent of her interest to the other directors before the company enters into the lease, either at a board meeting or by written or general notice.
options.C: She must obtain an ordinary resolution of the shareholders approving the lease, because a declaration to the board is not enough.
options.D: She may make her declaration at any time before the lease completes or within a reasonable time afterwards.
options.E: She need declare her interest only if one of the other directors asks her whether she has any interest in the transaction.

explanation:
Section 177(1) of the Companies Act 2006 requires a director who is in any way, directly or indirectly, interested in a proposed transaction or arrangement with the company to declare the nature and extent of that interest to the other directors. Her husband's majority stake in the landlord gives Priya at least an indirect interest in the proposed lease. Under s.177(2) the declaration may (but need not) be made at a meeting of the directors, or by notice in writing under s.184 or general notice under s.185, and under s.177(4) it must be made before the company enters into the transaction. None of the s.177(6) exceptions applies: the interest can reasonably be regarded as likely to give rise to a conflict, the other directors are not aware of it, and it does not concern her service contract.

A is wrong: s.177(1) catches interests held "directly or indirectly", so the fact that the shares are in her husband's name does not take Priya outside the duty.
C is wrong: s.177 requires a declaration to the other directors; it does not itself require shareholder approval of the transaction.
D is wrong: s.177(4) requires the declaration to be made before the company enters into the transaction or arrangement.
E is wrong: the duty is mandatory and does not depend on a request; the only exceptions are those in s.177(5) and (6).
key_rule: A director with any direct or indirect interest in a proposed transaction with the company must declare its nature and extent to the other directors before the company enters into it, unless a s.177(6) exception applies.
authority: Companies Act 2006, s.177

why_wrong.C: S.177 requires a declaration to the other directors; it does not itself require shareholder approval of the transaction.
why_wrong.D: S.177(4) requires the declaration to be made before the company enters into the transaction or arrangement.
why_wrong.E: The duty is mandatory and does not depend on a request; the only exceptions are those in s.177(5) and (6).

subject: Dispute Resolution
title: Default judgment after an acknowledgment of service (CPR 10.3, 15.4, 12.3)
scenario: Marsh Electrical Ltd issues a claim for a specified sum of £48,000 for unpaid invoices against Harlow Fabrication Ltd. The claim form and particulars of claim are served together. Harlow files an acknowledgment of service within the time allowed, stating that it intends to defend the whole claim. No extension of time has been agreed or ordered. Sixteen days after service of the particulars of claim, no defence has been filed, and Marsh's trainee suggests filing a request for default judgment straight away.
stem: Which of the following best describes the position?

options.A: Marsh may request default judgment now, because a defence must always be filed within 14 days after service of the particulars of claim.
options.B: Marsh can never obtain default judgment, because Harlow has filed an acknowledgment of service.
options.C: Marsh may not request default judgment now, because filing an acknowledgment of service automatically gives the parties a further agreed extension of 28 days under CPR 15.5.
options.D: Marsh may obtain default judgment now, but only by making an application under Part 23 supported by evidence.
options.E: Marsh may not yet obtain default judgment, because Harlow has 28 days after service of the particulars of claim to file its defence; judgment in default of defence is available only if that period has expired and no defence has been filed at the date judgment is entered.

explanation:
Under CPR 15.4(1) the general rule is that the period for filing a defence is 14 days after service of the particulars of claim or, if the defendant files an acknowledgment of service under Part 10, 28 days after service of the particulars of claim. Harlow has filed an acknowledgment of service, so it has 28 days. Under CPR 12.3(2)(a), judgment in default of defence may be obtained only where an acknowledgment of service has been filed but, at the date on which judgment is entered, a defence has not been filed, and the relevant time limit has expired. At day 16 the time for Harlow's defence has not expired, so a request would be premature.

A is wrong: the 14-day period in CPR 15.4(1)(a) applies only where no acknowledgment of service has been filed.
B is wrong: CPR 12.3(2)(a) expressly allows judgment in default of defence where an acknowledgment of service has been filed but no defence follows in time.
C is wrong: an extension under CPR 15.5 must be agreed between the parties (by up to 28 days) and the defendant must notify the court; nothing is agreed automatically.
D is wrong: for a claim for a specified amount of money, CPR 12.4(1)(a) allows default judgment by filing a request, and in any event the time for the defence has not yet expired.
key_rule: Once an acknowledgment of service is filed, the defence is due 28 days after service of the particulars of claim, and default judgment is available only if that period expires with no defence filed.

why_wrong.A: The 14-day period in CPR 15.4(1)(a) applies only where no acknowledgment of service has been filed.
why_wrong.B: CPR 12.3(2)(a) expressly allows judgment in default of defence where an acknowledgment of service has been filed but no defence follows in time.
why_wrong.C: An extension under CPR 15.5 must be agreed between the parties (by up to 28 days) and the defendant must notify the court; nothing is agreed automatically.
why_wrong.D: For a claim for a specified amount of money, CPR 12.4(1)(a) allows default judgment by filing a request, and in any event the time for the defence has not yet expired.

subject: Contract
title: Part payment of a debt (Foakes v Beer)
scenario: Gareth, a self-employed joiner, invoiced Ruth £8,000 for fitted wardrobes. The work is not disputed and payment was due on 1 June. Ruth, who could have paid in full, knew that Gareth urgently needed cash to pay his own suppliers. On 1 June she told him: "I will pay you £5,000 if you accept it in full settlement. If you don't, you'll get nothing." Gareth reluctantly signed a note, not executed as a deed, accepting £5,000 "in full and final settlement", and Ruth paid £5,000 by bank transfer that day. Two weeks later Gareth's solicitor wrote demanding the £3,000 balance.
stem: Which of the following best describes whether Gareth can recover the £3,000?

options.A: Gareth can recover the £3,000, because Ruth gave no fresh consideration for his promise to accept less, and on these facts there was no true accord making it inequitable for him to insist on the balance.
options.B: Gareth cannot recover the £3,000, because receiving prompt payment of part of the debt was a practical benefit to him and therefore good consideration.
options.C: Gareth cannot recover the £3,000, because his signed written note is binding on him even without consideration.
options.D: Gareth cannot recover the £3,000, because the Supreme Court in Rock Advertising Ltd v MWB Business Exchange Centres Ltd overruled Foakes v Beer.
options.E: Gareth cannot recover the £3,000, because promissory estoppel always prevents a creditor who has accepted part payment from suing for the balance.

explanation:
In Foakes v Beer (1884) 9 App Cas 605 the House of Lords affirmed the rule in Pinnel's Case that payment of a lesser sum on the day in satisfaction of a greater cannot be satisfaction of the whole. Ruth paid less than she owed, on the due date and in the ordinary way, so she gave no fresh consideration for Gareth's promise. An agreement not under seal is not enforceable without consideration. In D & C Builders Ltd v Rees [1966] 2 QB 617 the Court of Appeal held that equity will bar a creditor from claiming the balance only where it would be inequitable for him to insist on it, which requires a true accord; where the debtor exploits the creditor's known financial need with a threat to pay nothing, there is no true accord and the creditor may sue for the balance.

B is wrong: the House of Lords in Foakes v Beer held that the benefit a creditor gets from receiving part payment is not consideration, and the Supreme Court in Rock Advertising (para 18) noted that practical benefit was the very thing Foakes v Beer held inadequate.
C is wrong: Foakes v Beer confirms that an agreement not under seal to accept less requires consideration; signing a written note does not supply it.
D is wrong: in Rock Advertising the Supreme Court decided the case on the no oral modification clause and expressly declined to decide the consideration point, saying any overruling of Foakes v Beer should await an enlarged panel.
E is wrong: D & C Builders v Rees makes clear that the creditor is barred only where it would be inequitable to insist on his legal rights, and Ruth's pressure meant there was no true accord.
key_rule: Payment of a smaller sum on the due date is no consideration for a promise to forgo the balance, and equity will not bar the creditor where the settlement was extracted by pressure rather than by a true accord.
authority: Foakes v Beer (1884) 9 App Cas 605; D & C Builders Ltd v Rees [1966] 2 QB 617; Rock Advertising Ltd v MWB Business Exchange Centres Ltd [2018] UKSC 24

subject: Tort
title: Secondary victims after Paul v Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust
scenario: In March, Dr Okafor negligently failed to diagnose Daniel's serious heart disease when Daniel attended his GP surgery with chest pain. Eight months later, Daniel suffered a cardiac arrest at home and collapsed in front of his wife, Mei, who watched paramedics try and fail to resuscitate him. Mei has since been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder. It is accepted that Daniel would have survived with proper treatment, that Mei and Daniel had a close and loving marriage, and that a person of reasonable fortitude in Mei's position might have suffered a psychiatric illness.
stem: Which of the following best describes whether Mei can recover damages as a secondary victim?

options.A: Yes, because she had a close tie of love and affection with Daniel, was present at the scene and perceived his death with her own unaided senses.
options.B: No, because the collapse of a person from a heart condition is not, by objective standards, a sufficiently horrifying event.
options.C: No, because a secondary victim can recover only where she witnesses an accident or its immediate aftermath, and a death from an untreated disease is not an accident.
options.D: No, because Daniel's collapse happened eight months after the negligent omission, and a claim cannot be brought where the event witnessed is separated in time from the defendant's negligence.
options.E: Yes, provided that she can show her illness was caused by a sudden shock to her nervous system.

explanation:
In Paul v Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust [2024] UKSC 1 the majority of the Supreme Court held that the established rules for secondary victims apply to accidents, meaning an unexpected and unintended event which causes injury (or a risk of injury) to a victim by violent external means. Witnessing the death or manifestation of injury from a pre-existing disease which a doctor negligently failed to diagnose and treat is not analogous, and the persons a doctor ought reasonably to have in contemplation do not include close family members who might be psychologically affected by witnessing it. There is therefore no duty of care to Mei, however strongly she satisfies the other Alcock factors.

A is wrong: a close tie, presence and direct perception are required, but in Paul they were not enough because Mei did not witness an accident.
B is wrong: the majority in Paul rejected any separate requirement that the event witnessed be "horrifying".
D is wrong: the Supreme Court rejected the Court of Appeal's reading of Novo and saw no reason why the length of time between the negligence and the event witnessed should affect liability; the claim fails for the absence of an accident, not because of the gap in time.
E is wrong: the majority held that the law took a wrong turn in requiring proof of a "sudden shock to the nervous system", and in any event there was no accident.
key_rule: After Paul v Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust, a secondary victim must witness an accident or its immediate aftermath; witnessing death or injury from negligently untreated disease does not ground a claim.
authority: Paul v Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust [2024] UKSC 1

subject: Legal System of England and Wales
title: Court of Appeal and its own previous decisions (Young v Bristol Aeroplane)
scenario: In 2026 the Court of Appeal (Civil Division) hears an appeal in which the respondent, Callum Reid, relies on a 2019 decision of a three-judge Court of Appeal that is directly in point. The appellant, Seren Price, shows that in 2019 the court was not referred to, and plainly did not have in mind, a rule having statutory force which governs the point and points the other way. Because of the importance of the issue, a five-judge court has been convened. There is no relevant decision of the House of Lords or Supreme Court.
stem: Which of the following best describes whether the Court of Appeal may decline to follow its 2019 decision?

options.A: It may not, because the Court of Appeal is bound by its own previous decisions in every case, and only the Supreme Court can depart from them.
options.B: It may, because a five-judge court has greater power than a three-judge court and can overrule the earlier decision.
options.C: It may, because the Court of Appeal can depart from any of its own previous decisions whenever it is satisfied that the decision was wrong.
options.D: It may, because a decision given in ignorance of a statutory provision binding on the court is given per incuriam, and the Court of Appeal is not bound to follow its own per incuriam decisions.
options.E: It may not, because the 2019 decision has not been expressly overruled by the House of Lords or the Supreme Court.

explanation:
In Young v Bristol Aeroplane Co Ltd [1944] KB 718 the Court of Appeal held that it is bound to follow its own previous decisions, subject to three exceptions: (1) it must decide which of two conflicting decisions of its own to follow; (2) it must refuse to follow a decision of its own which, though not expressly overruled, cannot stand with a decision of the House of Lords; and (3) it is not bound to follow a decision of its own given per incuriam. The court gave as the example of a per incuriam decision one given in ignorance of the terms of a statute or a rule having the force of a statute. The 2019 decision falls within that third exception.

A is wrong: Young recognises exceptions to the general rule, including decisions given per incuriam.
B is wrong: Young held that the full court has no greater powers than a division of three, so what a division cannot do the full court cannot do either.
C is wrong: Young rejected any general power to depart from a previous decision merely because the court considers it wrong.
E is wrong: express overruling is not required for the exceptions to apply, and the relevant exception here is that the earlier decision was given per incuriam.
key_rule: The Court of Appeal (Civil Division) is bound by its own decisions unless they conflict, cannot stand with a House of Lords decision, or were given per incuriam; a larger panel has no greater power.
authority: Young v Bristol Aeroplane Co Ltd [1944] KB 718, [1944] EWCA Civ 1

why_wrong.B: Young held that the full court has no greater powers than a division of three, so what a division cannot do the full court cannot do either.
why_wrong.C: Young rejected any general power to depart from a previous decision merely because the court considers it wrong.
why_wrong.E: Express overruling is not required for the exceptions to apply, and the relevant exception here is that the earlier decision was given per incuriam.

subject: Constitutional & Administrative Law
title: Effect of a declaration of incompatibility (HRA 1998 ss.3-4)
scenario: In proceedings in the High Court, Farah Siddiqui argues that a section of an Act of Parliament breaches her right to respect for private and family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The judge concludes that the provision cannot be read and given effect in a way that is compatible with Article 8, and makes a declaration of incompatibility.
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of the declaration?

options.A: The provision becomes void from the date of the declaration and can no longer be enforced against anyone.
options.B: The provision remains valid and continues in operation and force, the declaration does not bind the parties, and a Minister may make a remedial order if he considers there are compelling reasons to do so.
options.C: The High Court must disapply the provision in Farah's case and decide the claim as if the provision did not exist.
options.D: Parliament is legally required to amend or repeal the provision within six months of the declaration.
options.E: The declaration is of no effect, because only the Supreme Court may make a declaration of incompatibility.

explanation:
Section 3(1) of the Human Rights Act 1998 requires legislation to be read and given effect compatibly with Convention rights so far as it is possible to do so, but s.3(2)(b) provides that this does not affect the validity, continuing operation or enforcement of incompatible primary legislation. Where a compatible reading is not possible, the court may make a declaration of incompatibility under s.4(2). Section 4(6) provides that the declaration does not affect the validity, continuing operation or enforcement of the provision and is not binding on the parties. Section 10 then allows a Minister of the Crown who considers there are compelling reasons to amend the legislation by remedial order to remove the incompatibility.

A is wrong: s.4(6)(a) states that the declaration does not affect the validity of the provision.
C is wrong: the provision continues in operation and must still be enforced (s.3(2)(b) and s.4(6)(a)); the court cannot strike down or disapply primary legislation under the Act.
D is wrong: nothing in ss.4 or 10 obliges Parliament to act; s.10 gives a Minister a discretionary power to make a remedial order.
E is wrong: s.4(5)(e) lists the High Court, as well as the Court of Appeal and Supreme Court, among the courts that may make a declaration in England and Wales.
key_rule: A declaration of incompatibility under s.4 HRA 1998 leaves the provision valid, operative and enforceable and does not bind the parties; change is left to Parliament or a Minister's remedial order under s.10.
authority: Human Rights Act 1998, ss.3, 4 and 10

why_wrong.A: S.4(6)(a) states that the declaration does not affect the validity of the provision.
why_wrong.C: The provision continues in operation and must still be enforced (s.3(2)(b) and s.4(6)(a)); the court cannot strike down or disapply primary legislation under the Act.
why_wrong.D: Nothing in ss.4 or 10 obliges Parliament to act; s.10 gives a Minister a discretionary power to make a remedial order.
why_wrong.E: S.4(5)(e) lists the High Court, as well as the Court of Appeal and Supreme Court, among the courts that may make a declaration in England and Wales.

subject: Ethics & Professional Conduct
title: Acting against a former client whose confidential information you hold (SRA Code paras 6.3-6.5)
scenario: Two years ago Omar, a solicitor at Ashby Cole LLP, advised Lyndon Ltd on refinancing its debts and learned detailed confidential information about its cash flow and lenders. That retainer has ended. Petra Hale now asks the firm to act for her in a claim against Lyndon Ltd for an unpaid debt, and Lyndon's ability to pay is likely to be central to her tactics. The firm still holds Lyndon's file, and the information on it is material to Petra's matter. Petra says she is happy to sign anything to get Omar's help.
stem: Which of the following best describes whether Ashby Cole LLP may act for Petra?

options.A: It may act, because Lyndon Ltd is a former client and the duty of confidentiality ended when that retainer ended.
options.B: It may act and should tell Petra what it knows about Lyndon's finances, because a solicitor must make a client aware of all information material to the matter.
options.C: It may act, provided Petra gives informed consent, given or evidenced in writing, to the firm acting.
options.D: It may never act against a former client in any circumstances.
options.E: It may act only if effective measures have been taken which result in there being no real risk of disclosure of Lyndon's confidential information, or Lyndon gives informed consent, given or evidenced in writing, to the firm acting, including to any measures taken to protect its information.

explanation:
Paragraph 6.3 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs requires solicitors to keep the affairs of current and former clients confidential unless disclosure is required or permitted by law or the client consents. Paragraph 6.5 provides that a solicitor must not act for a client in a matter where that client has an interest adverse to another current or former client of the solicitor or their business, for whom confidential information material to the matter is held, unless (a) effective measures have been taken which result in there being no real risk of disclosure, or (b) the client whose information is held has given informed consent, given or evidenced in writing, to the solicitor acting, including to any protective measures. Petra's interests are adverse to Lyndon's and the firm holds material confidential information, so it can act only if one of those conditions is met.

A is wrong: para 6.3 expressly extends confidentiality to former clients.
B is wrong: the para 6.4 duty to tell a client of material information does not override the para 6.3 duty to keep Lyndon's affairs confidential, which applies unless the law requires or permits disclosure or Lyndon consents; this tension is why para 6.5 restricts acting at all.
C is wrong: under para 6.5(b) the relevant consent is that of the client whose confidential information is held (Lyndon), not the new client.
D is wrong: para 6.5 permits acting where there is no real risk of disclosure through effective measures, or with the informed written consent of the former client.
key_rule: A solicitor may act against a current or former client whose material confidential information they hold only if effective measures leave no real risk of disclosure or that client gives informed consent, given or evidenced in writing.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, paras 6.3 to 6.5

why_wrong.B: The para 6.4 duty to tell a client of material information does not override the para 6.3 duty to keep Lyndon's affairs confidential, which applies unless the law requires or permits disclosure or Lyndon consents; this tension is why para 6.5 restricts acting at all.
why_wrong.C: Under para 6.5(b) the relevant consent is that of the client whose confidential information is held (Lyndon), not the new client.
why_wrong.D: Para 6.5 permits acting where there is no real risk of disclosure through effective measures, or with the informed written consent of the former client.

subject: Property Practice
title: Failure to complete and the notice to complete (SCS 5th ed, condition 6.8)
scenario: Aisha is selling her flat in Croydon to Ben. The contract incorporates the Standard Conditions of Sale (Fifth Edition, 2018 Revision) without amendment, except for a special condition under which Ben paid a deposit of 5% of the purchase price on exchange. Completion was due on a Monday, but Ben's lender failed to release the mortgage funds and he did not complete. Aisha is ready, able and willing to complete. At 10am on the Tuesday, Aisha's solicitor hand-delivers a notice to complete to the office of Ben's solicitor.
stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of the notice to complete?

options.A: Ben must complete within ten working days of the notice, counting the Tuesday on which it was given as the first day.
options.B: Ben must complete within twenty working days of the notice, as that is the standard period for completion under the Standard Conditions.
options.C: Ben must complete within ten working days of the notice, excluding the day it was given, time is of the essence, and he must forthwith pay a further deposit to bring the total to 10% of the price.
options.D: The notice is invalid, because Aisha's solicitor should have served it on Ben personally rather than on his solicitor.
options.E: Ben must complete within ten working days, but time is not of the essence, so Aisha's only remedy for further delay is compensation at the contract rate.

explanation:
Under condition 6.8.1, at any time after the time applicable under condition 6.1.2 on completion date, a party who is ready, able and willing to complete may give the other a notice to complete. Aisha meets that test and the notice is given the day after completion date. Condition 6.8.2 requires the parties to complete within ten working days of giving the notice, excluding the day on which it is given, and makes time of the essence for this purpose. Condition 6.8.3(b) adds that a buyer who paid a deposit of less than 10% must, on receipt of the notice, forthwith pay a further deposit equal to the balance of that 10%. Giving a notice to a party's conveyancer has the same effect as giving it to the party (condition 1.3.2). If Ben then fails to complete in accordance with the notice, condition 7.4.2 allows Aisha to rescind, forfeit and keep the deposit, resell and claim damages.

A is wrong: condition 6.8.2 expressly excludes the day on which the notice is given.
B is wrong: twenty working days after the date of the contract is the default completion date under condition 6.1.1, not the period allowed by a notice to complete.
D is wrong: condition 1.3.2 provides that giving a notice to a party's conveyancer has the same effect as giving it to that party.
E is wrong: condition 6.8.2 makes time of the essence once a notice to complete is given, and condition 7.4 gives the seller the right to rescind if the buyer fails to comply.
key_rule: Under SCS 6.8, a notice to complete requires completion within ten working days (excluding the day given), time being of the essence; a buyer who paid under 10% must top up the deposit immediately.

subject: Wills & Administration of Estates
title: Revocation of a will by marriage and the expectation of marriage exception (Wills Act 1837 s.18)
scenario: In 2024, Marcus made a valid will leaving his whole estate to his fiancee, Leila Haddad. The will states: 'I make this will in expectation of my marriage to Leila Haddad and I intend that it shall not be revoked by that marriage.' Marcus and Leila later separated without marrying. In 2026 Marcus married Sofia Brennan. He made no further will and has recently died. Leila claims the estate under the 2024 will.
stem: Which of the following best describes the status of the 2024 will?

options.A: It remains valid, because it was expressly made in expectation of marriage and stated that it should not be revoked by marriage.
options.B: It remains valid, because a will can only be revoked by a later will or by its deliberate destruction.
options.C: It is revoked only as to the gift to Leila, and the rest of the will takes effect.
options.D: It remains valid, because Marcus did not marry within twelve months of making it.
options.E: It is revoked by Marcus's marriage to Sofia, because the protection for a will made in expectation of marriage applies only to marriage to the particular person named.

explanation:
Section 18(1) of the Wills Act 1837 provides that, subject to subsections (2) to (5), a will is revoked by the testator's marriage. Section 18(3) saves a will only where it appears from the will that, when it was made, the testator was expecting to be married to a particular person and intended that the will should not be revoked by the marriage, and even then it is not revoked only by his marriage to that person. Marcus's will satisfies s.18(3) as regards Leila, but he never married Leila. His marriage to Sofia is not covered, so s.18(1) applies and the will is revoked.

A is wrong: s.18(3) protects the will only against marriage to the particular person the testator expected to marry, here Leila, not Sofia.
B is wrong: s.18(1) makes marriage itself a ground of revocation, operating automatically.
C is wrong: partial survival of dispositions under s.18(4) also depends on the testator's marriage to the particular person contemplated, so it cannot save the gift on a marriage to someone else.
D is wrong: s.18 contains no twelve-month time limit; the question is whether the marriage is to the particular person named in the will.
key_rule: Marriage revokes a will under s.18(1) Wills Act 1837 unless the will shows it was made expecting marriage to a particular person and intending it not to be revoked, and that saving applies only on marriage to that person.
authority: Wills Act 1837, s.18

why_wrong.A: S.18(3) protects the will only against marriage to the particular person the testator expected to marry, here Leila, not Sofia.
why_wrong.B: S.18(1) makes marriage itself a ground of revocation, operating automatically.
why_wrong.C: Partial survival of dispositions under s.18(4) also depends on the testator's marriage to the particular person contemplated, so it cannot save the gift on a marriage to someone else.
why_wrong.D: S.18 contains no twelve-month time limit; the question is whether the marriage is to the particular person named in the will.

subject: Solicitors Accounts
title: Client account must not be used as a banking facility (SRA Accounts Rules, rule 3.3)
scenario: Hartley & Rowe LLP acted for Tomasz on the sale of the freehold premises of his former café. Completion took place last week and the firm still holds the £40,000 balance of the sale proceeds in client account. Its bill has been paid. Tomasz is between bank accounts and asks the firm to keep the money in client account for the next six months and, on his instructions, pay his household bills, his suppliers' invoices for a new business and his daughter's university fees.
stem: Which of the following best describes how the firm should respond?

options.A: It should decline and return the balance to Tomasz promptly, because a client account must not be used to provide banking facilities and payments through it must be in respect of the firm's delivery of regulated services.
options.B: It may agree, provided Tomasz gives written instructions for each payment, because withdrawals may be made following receipt of instructions from the client.
options.C: It may agree, provided it accounts to Tomasz for a fair sum of interest on the money while it is held.
options.D: It may agree, provided the firm's COFA approves the arrangement in advance and signs off each payment.
options.E: It may agree, because the money came into client account in connection with a matter on which the firm acted for Tomasz.

explanation:
Rule 3.3 of the SRA Accounts Rules provides that a firm must not use a client account to provide banking facilities to clients or third parties, and that payments into, and transfers or withdrawals from, a client account must be in respect of the delivery by the firm of regulated services. The sale is complete and the firm's bill is paid, so paying Tomasz's household bills, new business invoices and university fees would not relate to any regulated service the firm is delivering. In addition, rule 2.5 requires client money to be returned promptly to the client as soon as there is no longer any proper reason to hold it.

B is wrong: rule 5.1(b) permits withdrawals on the client's instructions, but that does not override the separate prohibition in rule 3.3 on using client account as a banking facility.
C is wrong: the duty to account for interest under rule 7 applies to money properly held; it does not make an otherwise prohibited arrangement permissible.
D is wrong: no approval by the COFA can authorise a use of client account that rule 3.3 prohibits.
E is wrong: once the transaction is completed and the bill paid, there is no proper reason to hold the money, and the proposed payments are unconnected with the delivery of regulated services.
key_rule: A client account must not be used to provide banking facilities, and every payment into or out of it must be in respect of the firm's delivery of regulated services (SRA Accounts Rules, rule 3.3).
authority: SRA Accounts Rules, rules 2.5, 3.3, 5.1 and 7

why_wrong.C: The duty to account for interest under rule 7 applies to money properly held; it does not make an otherwise prohibited arrangement permissible.
why_wrong.D: No approval by the COFA can authorise a use of client account that rule 3.3 prohibits.
why_wrong.E: Once the transaction is completed and the bill paid, there is no proper reason to hold the money, and the proposed payments are unconnected with the delivery of regulated services.

subject: Land Law
title: Overreaching on payment to two trustees and a beneficiary in actual occupation (LPA 1925 ss.2 and 27; City of London BS v Flegg)
scenario: Hamid and Rania are the registered proprietors of a freehold house in Reading. Rania's mother, Margaret, contributed a third of the purchase price on the understanding that she would have a share in the house, and she has lived there with them ever since. There is no entry on the register referring to Margaret's interest. Without telling Margaret, Hamid and Rania grant a legal charge of the house to Northgate Bank plc, which pays the loan to both of them jointly. The bank makes no enquiry of Margaret. Hamid and Rania have defaulted, and the bank seeks possession. Margaret argues that her beneficial interest binds the bank.
stem: Which of the following best describes Margaret's position against the bank?

options.A: Her interest binds the bank as an interest of a person in actual occupation, because no enquiry was made of her before the charge was granted.
options.B: Her interest binds the bank, because a beneficiary in actual occupation must consent before trustees can mortgage the land.
options.C: Her interest binds the bank, because the bank had constructive notice of her occupation and a purchaser with notice takes subject to equitable interests.
options.D: The bank takes free of her interest, because the loan money was paid to two trustees, so her interest was overreached and her occupation does not preserve it against the bank.
options.E: The bank takes free of her interest, because a contribution to the purchase price gives a family member only a personal licence to occupy.

explanation:
Under s.2(1)(ii) of the Law of Property Act 1925, a conveyance to a purchaser of a legal estate by trustees of land overreaches equitable interests capable of being overreached, whether or not the purchaser has notice, if the requirements of s.27 about payment of capital money are complied with. Section 27(2) requires capital money to be paid to or applied by the direction of at least two trustees (unless the trustee is a trust corporation). In City of London Building Society v Flegg [1988] AC 54, on materially similar facts, the House of Lords held that a legal charge granted by two trustees, with the money paid to both, overreached the interests of beneficiaries in actual occupation. A chargee by way of legal mortgage is a purchaser for these purposes. Lord Templeman said the interests 'cannot at one and the same time be overreached and ... be overriding interests', and Lord Oliver explained that, once overreached, the occupier's rights subsist only against the equity of redemption, not against the chargee. Williams & Glyn's Bank v Boland was distinguished because the money there was paid to a sole trustee. Margaret's interest is therefore overreached and the bank takes free of it.

A is wrong: actual occupation (now Land Registration Act 2002, Sch 3, para 2; under the 1925 Act, s.70(1)(g), the provision considered in Flegg) protects only an interest that subsists at the time of the disposition, and Margaret's interest was overreached by the charge.
B is wrong: Flegg rejected the argument that a purchaser from trustees must ensure that a beneficiary in actual occupation consents.
C is wrong: s.2(1) overreaches qualifying interests 'whether or not he has notice thereof', so notice is irrelevant where capital money is paid to two trustees.
E is wrong: Margaret's contribution gave her a beneficial interest under a trust, as in Flegg; the point is that this interest was overreached, not that it never existed.
key_rule: Where capital money is paid to at least two trustees, a beneficiary's interest is overreached and shifts to the proceeds and equity of redemption, even if the beneficiary is in actual occupation.
authority: Law of Property Act 1925, ss.2 and 27; City of London Building Society v Flegg [1988] AC 54 (HL)

why_wrong.A: Actual occupation (now Land Registration Act 2002, Sch 3, para 2; under the 1925 Act, s.70(1)(g), the provision considered in Flegg) protects only an interest that subsists at the time of the disposition, and Margaret's interest was overreached by the charge.
why_wrong.B: Flegg rejected the argument that a purchaser from trustees must ensure that a beneficiary in actual occupation consents.
why_wrong.C: S.2(1) overreaches qualifying interests 'whether or not he has notice thereof', so notice is irrelevant where capital money is paid to two trustees.
why_wrong.E: Margaret's contribution gave her a beneficial interest under a trust, as in Flegg; the point is that this interest was overreached, not that it never existed.

subject: Trusts
title: Certainty of intention and precatory words
scenario: Eleanor died last year. Her will, which is valid, leaves £60,000 'to my sister Joan absolutely, in the hope and confidence that she will use it as she sees fit for the benefit of my nephews, Callum and Rory'. Nothing else in the will refers to the gift or to the nephews. Joan has told Callum and Rory that she plans to spend the money on a round-the-world cruise. They wish to argue that Joan holds the £60,000 on trust for them.
stem: Which of the following best describes Joan's entitlement to the £60,000?

options.A: Joan holds it on trust for Callum and Rory, because no particular form of words is needed to create a trust.
options.B: Joan takes it absolutely, because the words used express a hope rather than an imperative obligation, so there is no certainty of intention to create a trust.
options.C: Joan holds it on trust for Callum and Rory, because the court will give effect to the testator's evident wish to benefit her family.
options.D: The gift fails and falls into Eleanor's residuary estate, because the reference to the nephews makes the testator's intention uncertain.
options.E: Joan holds it on resulting trust for Eleanor's estate, because the intended trust for the nephews is incompletely constituted.

explanation:
An express trust requires certainty of intention. In Paul v Constance [1977] 1 WLR 527, the Court of Appeal accepted the statement in Snell that the words relied on 'must be so used that on the whole they ought to be construed as imperative', while also noting that no particular form of expression is necessary if on the whole it can be gathered that a trust was intended. Scarman LJ accepted that there must be clear evidence from what is said or done of an intention to create a trust. Eleanor's gift is expressed to be absolute, and the words 'in the hope and confidence that she will use it as she sees fit' express a hope and leave the matter to Joan's discretion; they do not impose a binding obligation. Read as a whole, the will shows no intention to create a trust, so Joan takes the money absolutely, subject at most to a moral obligation.

A is wrong: although no particular form of words is required, the words used must still, on the whole, be imperative; here they are not.
